Jesus foretells the Gentiles will mock, scourge and crucify him (Matt 20:19); the governor's soldiers do so and crucify him (Matt 27:27, 27:35).
An assault of both Gentiles and Jews with their rulers, to stone Paul and Barnabas.

Took counsel with the Pharisees to destroy him.; "began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus"; 'They sent their disciples to Him along with the Herodians.' (Matt 22:16). **An unlikely pairing** -- a party of the law with a party of Herod -- which Mark 3:6 also records taking counsel together.

James speaks last and decisively at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:13-19) and is the one Paul and his company go in to, with the elders present, on returning to Jerusalem (Acts 21:18). The text never calls him 'leader' outright, so this is inferred from his role in both scenes.

The letter names only 'James' with no further identification, and which James is meant is unsettled: tradition and the prominence of a Jerusalem-based James elsewhere in Acts (15:13, 21:18) and Galatians point to James the Lord's brother, but James son of Zebedee or James son of Alphaeus cannot be ruled out from the letter's own text.

'the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him' (John 5:18); 'He did not want to travel in Judea, because the Jews there were trying to kill Him' (John 7:1); 'the Jews again picked up stones to stone Him' (John 10:31).

'the Jews conspired to kill him' (Acts 9:23); at Iconium 'the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone them' (Acts 14:5); 'the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. More than forty of them were involved in this plot' (Acts 23:12-13).

A second, later letter to this congregation, distinct from Paul's Ephesians already recorded in the epistles batch. 'John, To the seven churches' (Rev 1:4) names the sender; the address list (Rev 1:11) and the opening of the individual letter (Rev 2:1) name the church, though not in the same verse as 'John'.
